anchor: Come, dear children, let us away
title: The Forsaken Merman: date and source
short: Published in Arnold's first book, The Strayed Reveller, and Other Poems (1849), the poem retells a Scandinavian legend of a sea-king deserted by his human wife.
body: Arnold's first collection appeared anonymously as by 'A.' in 1849, and early reviewers found much of the volume obscure and aloof, but this poem was admired, and Swinburne later praised its lyric beauty. The story of a woman who marries a merman, bears him children, then returns to land and church and will not go back, is found across Danish, German and Slavonic folklore. The closest analogue is the Danish ballad 'Agnete og Havmanden', also told in a prose version in J. M. Thiele's Danish folk-tales, where the woman is called Grethe; because Arnold's heroine is Margaret, some have thought Thiele's account his real source. Arnold named no source, and the question has been revisited by Herbert Wright (1918) and Clyde C. Hyder (1980); Hans Christian Andersen and George Borrow have also been suggested as intermediaries. Arnold's change is decisive: the tale is told not by the narrator of a ballad but by the abandoned merman himself, speaking to his children.

title: The merman as speaker
short: The whole poem is the merman's speech to his children, so we hear the desertion only from the side of the one left behind.
body: Arnold gives the legend the shape of a dramatic monologue with a silent audience, the merman's children. This throws the reader's sympathy, unusually, toward the pagan sea-world rather than the Christian town. The merman is tender, patient and bewildered rather than demonic; his repeated orders to 'come away' alternate with his inability to stop calling. Critics have read the poem as one of Arnold's early dramatisations of divided allegiance: between a natural, unreflective life (the sea) and a life governed by conscience and religion (the church), with the poet's sympathies notably uncertain. Margaret herself never speaks except through reported words and her song in the town, so the poem's centre is a loss described from outside.

title: wild white horses
short: The 'white horses' are breaking waves with white crests, a common idiom made literal and animate here.
body: 'White horses' for white-capped waves was an established English idiom (recorded in the OED). Arnold revives the dead metaphor by giving the horses verbs proper to animals: they 'Champ and chafe and toss in the spray', and later 'foam and fret' (l. 21). The image belongs to the merman's world, where the sea is a living, restless household rather than a scene. The heavy alliteration and the run of stressed monosyllables imitate the surf, and the horses' impatience presses on the children's calls to their mother: the tide is turning and they cannot wait.

title: Margaret
short: Arnold gives the human mother an English, Christian name, replacing the Agnete of the Danish ballad.
body: In the Danish ballad the woman is Agnete (Agnes); Arnold renames her Margaret, a name with strong Christian associations (St Margaret of Antioch, among others) and a domestic English ring. The doubled cry is the poem's first refrain, and it returns at l. 22 and in the merman's 'Margaret, hist!' at the church window (l. 77). Some readers have connected the name with the 'Marguerite' of Arnold's Switzerland lyrics, written around the same time, where another lover is lost across a dividing sea; the connection is suggestive rather than proven, but both poems turn on estrangement that neither party can undo.

title: Refrain and irregular metre
short: The question 'was it yesterday?' recurs like a ballad refrain and suggests the merman's confused sense of time.
body: The poem is written in irregular, mostly four-stress lines with very varied line lengths and rhyme, closer to the free 'Pindaric' lyric than to the strict ballad stanza; a contemporary American reviewer called it a wild, irregular melody. The refrain question 'was it yesterday?' frames the memories of the bells and of Margaret's departure. It may be a real uncertainty: in many sea-legends time passes differently under the water, and the merman cannot tell whether a day or years have gone by. It also expresses grief that keeps the loss always recent. The verse loosens and tightens with emotion, moving from the long, hypnotic catalogue of the caverns to the clipped commands 'Come away, come away!'

title: The sea-caverns
short: A long catalogue of the undersea world, built on anaphora ('Where ... Where ...'), sets a timeless, sleepy paradise against the town's bells.
body: The sentence beginning 'Children dear, was it yesterday' runs for sixteen lines before its question mark, carried by repeated 'Where' clauses. The undersea world is calm and unhurried: the winds are 'all asleep', the 'spent lights' (sunlight exhausted by its passage through water) 'quiver and gleam', the sea-beasts graze like cattle in 'the ooze of their pasture-ground'. Everything here is self-contained and cyclical; even the whales sail 'Round the world for ever and aye', echoing ballad diction ('for ever and aye'). Against this enclosed paradise the single intruding sound is the 'silver bell' of the church, which first draws Margaret away. The passage is often admired as the most purely musical in Arnold's verse.

title: with unshut eye
short: The whales never close their eyes: an image of sleepless, endless, unreflecting life.
body: Arnold imagines the whales sailing round the world with eyes that never shut, a detail of fancy rather than natural history. The image extends the timelessness of the sea-world: nothing there sleeps, ends, or turns inward. 'The sea-snakes ... Dry their mail and bask in the brine' (ll. 41-2) is a similarly playful paradox, since 'mail' (armour, here scales) can hardly dry in salt water. These touches make the undersea world strange and slightly comic, and they distinguish it from the town, which is ruled by clock-like church time: Easter, prayers, bells.

sources.cite: Kenneth Allott, ed., The Poems of Matthew Arnold (Longman Annotated English Poets, 1965; 2nd edn, ed. Miriam Allott, 1979), notes to 'The Forsaken Merman'

title: the church bell
short: The bell is the voice of Christian time calling Margaret back to land, prayer and the fear for her soul.
body: Church bells heard under the sea are a recurring motif in legends of drowned or enchanted people; here they announce Easter and draw Margaret 'up through the clear green sea'. The bell is 'far-off' and 'silver', beautiful to the merman, who does not grasp what it means. It belongs to the same cluster as 'the priest, and the bell, and the holy well' (l. 91) in Margaret's later song, the apparatus of a parish religion. The poem stages the contrast without simply taking sides: the bell brings Margaret salvation, as she believes, and brings the merman and his children abandonment.

sources.cite: Kenneth Allott, ed., The Poems of Matthew Arnold (Longman Annotated English Poets, 1965; 2nd edn, ed. Miriam Allott, 1979), notes to 'The Forsaken Merman'

title: Easter-time; 'lose my poor soul'
short: Margaret returns for the Easter festival because she fears that by living with a merman she will lose her soul.
body: In folklore the merfolk were often imagined as beings without immortal souls, an idea Arnold could have met in many forms (Hans Christian Andersen's 'The Little Mermaid', 1837, turns on a mermaid's longing for a soul). Margaret's words, 'I lose my poor soul, Merman! here with thee', make the conflict explicitly religious: to stay in the sea is damnation. Easter, the feast of resurrection and the season of annual communion, is the occasion that pulls her back. The phrase 'in the world' marks the land as the realm of human, historical, Christian time, quite distinct from the sea's eternity.

title: sate
short: 'Sate' is an archaic past tense of 'sit', used here for its antique, ballad flavour.
body: 'Sate' was a common literary spelling of the past tense 'sat' into the nineteenth century, and Arnold uses it again at l. 76 ('She sate by the pillar'). Together with forms like 'aye', 'hie' (l. 133, 'go quickly') and 'anon' (l. 101, 'presently, at once'), it gives the poem the colouring of an old ballad. The 'red gold throne in the heart of the sea' is equally conventional, the fairy-tale splendour of a sea-king's hall, set against the 'little grey church' of the town.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary

title: hist
short: 'Hist' is an exclamation used to attract attention quietly, like 'psst'.
body: The merman and his children, standing outside the church 'in the cold blowing airs', climb on the graves and peer through the 'small leaded panes'. Their whispered 'hist!' is a lovely touch of shyness: the sea-folk are intruders in sacred space. The scene is the dramatic climax of the poem, since Margaret does not look up: 'her eyes were seal'd to the holy book'. The graveyard setting quietly reminds us of the mortality Margaret has accepted along with her soul.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary

title: eyes seal'd to the holy book
short: Margaret's refusal to look up can be read as devotion, as hardness, or as a struggle she must win by not looking.
body: 'Seal'd' suggests both fixed attention and closed sight, a person blind to everything but the page. The line invites different readings. On one view Arnold criticises a narrow religion that seals its followers off from natural affection; Margaret's 'faithless' desertion of her children is the cost of orthodoxy. On another, her steadfastness is heroic and the merman cannot understand it. The next section complicates both readings, since Margaret is not at peace: at her spinning-wheel she sings joyfully but then stares at the sea and weeps. Many critics see here a version of Arnold's lifelong sense of being caught between two worlds, neither fully satisfying.

title: Margaret's song in the town
short: Margaret's song praises the human world: street, child, priest, bell, holy well, spinning-wheel and sunlight.
body: The catalogue mirrors the merman's catalogue of the caverns, so the two worlds are given equal lyrical weight. Margaret's joys are social and domestic: 'the humming street', 'the child with its toy', ordinary labour at 'the wheel where I spun'. The 'holy well' recalls the many wells associated with saints in medieval and folk Christianity. Most striking is 'the blessed light of the sun', which the sea-world lacks, since there only 'spent lights' reach. The spinning-wheel has a long literary history as the emblem of a woman's settled, domestic life.

sources.cite: Kenneth Allott, ed., The Poems of Matthew Arnold (Longman Annotated English Poets, 1965; 2nd edn, ed. Miriam Allott, 1979), notes to 'The Forsaken Merman'

title: the stare at the sea
short: When the wheel stops, Margaret steals to the window and stares at the sea, weeping for her lost mermaid daughter.
body: This passage, imagined by the merman since he cannot see it, gives Margaret an inner life of regret. The 'whizzing wheel stands still' and the spindle drops: her domestic contentment breaks off. Her grief is focused on 'the cold strange eyes of a little Mermaiden' and 'her golden hair', the child she combed in the sea (l. 53). The 'cold strange eyes' suggest that the child already seems alien to her, half of another world. The irregular shortening of lines ('A long, long sigh') slows the verse to match the stillness.

sources.cite: Kenneth Allott, ed., The Poems of Matthew Arnold (Longman Annotated English Poets, 1965; 2nd edn, ed. Miriam Allott, 1979), notes to 'The Forsaken Merman'

title: A ceiling of amber, / A pavement of pearl
short: Seen from below, the stormy surface of the sea becomes a ceiling of amber and the sea-bed a pavement of pearl.
body: The final sections shift into short, dactylic and anapaestic two-stress lines, giving a lilting, song-like close. While the waves 'roar and whirl' above, the merfolk will have 'A ceiling of amber' over them and 'A pavement of pearl' beneath, a fairy-tale image of riches in which the amber may suggest light glinting through the water. Their song, 'Here came a mortal, / But faithless was she!', turns the story into a legend told against Margaret. In the closing section it becomes 'cruel is she!', a significant hardening of judgment.

sources.cite: Kenneth Allott, ed., The Poems of Matthew Arnold (Longman Annotated English Poets, 1965; 2nd edn, ed. Miriam Allott, 1979), notes to 'The Forsaken Merman'

title: sea-stocks; broom
short: Sea-stock is a coastal wild flower; broom is a yellow-flowered shrub of heaths. Both locate the town on a real coast.
body: The sea stock (Matthiola sinuata) is a fragrant, purple-flowered plant of sand-dunes and sea-cliffs; Arnold's 'sandy down' is a dune. In the last section (l. 129), 'heaths starr'd with broom' refers to the shrub Cytisus scoparius, whose bright yellow flowers spot the heath like stars. Such precise botanical details anchor the legend in an English or Northern European shoreline, with its 'white-wall'd town' and 'little grey church', rather than in a fairy-tale nowhere.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary

anchor: Up the creeks we will hie
title: hie
short: 'Hie' is an archaic verb meaning to go quickly, hasten.
body: The word belongs, like 'sate' and 'anon', to the poem's old-ballad vocabulary. In the final section the merman promises that the family will come up at midnight, at low spring tides, to gaze at the sleeping town, and then 'come back down'. 'Blanch'd sands' (l. 131), sands whitened by the moonlight, and 'a gloom' thrown by the high rocks continue the moonlit, hushed atmosphere. The return visits will be secret and repeated, a ritual of longing.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary

title: 'The kings of the sea': the ending
short: The poem ends with the merfolk's song in which 'faithless' becomes 'cruel' and 'alone' becomes 'lonely for ever'.
body: The two final stanzas end with parallel quatrains. The first: 'Here came a mortal, / But faithless was she! / And alone dwell for ever / The kings of the sea.' The second: 'There dwells a loved one, / But cruel is she! / She left lonely for ever / The kings of the sea.' The small changes ('mortal' to 'loved one', 'faithless' to 'cruel', 'alone' to 'lonely') shift the emphasis from a broken bond to a permanent wound. The merman's dignity ('kings') is preserved, but the poem closes on desolation rather than resolution. Critics continue to differ over whether the poem's sympathy finally lies with the sea or with the church.
